title: Monroe v. City of Charlottesville
lead: A proposed class representative’s uncertain involvement defeated certification, while separate rulings rejected two of his constitutional theories about a police DNA investigation.

actors.name: Larry Monroe
actors.role: Man approached for DNA who sought to represent a class

actors.name: Officer Mooney
actors.role: Officer who approached Monroe at home

proceedings: District court: dismissed two constitutional theories, left others pending, then denied certification after evidentiary submissions.
Remaining individual claims voluntarily dismissed with an agreement not to refile.
Fourth Circuit: affirmed certification denial and challenged dismissals.
limits: The case does not decide voluntarily dismissed claims on their merits or establish every DNA collection consensual. Its reported route to appellate finality is historical, not certification of later finality doctrine.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A serial-assault investigation uses descriptions and other leads
sections.cue: Introduce the police contacts and Monroe’s theories.
paragraphs: Beginning in spring 2002, Charlottesville police investigated a serial rapist. Several victims consistently described a youthful-looking Black man, and officers had composite images and the assailant’s DNA. They asked people matching the general description and lacking a sample on file for specimens, contacting 190 Black men over several years. The opinion described composite images, tips, records, and other information, while preserving possible minimal exceptions rather than asserting identical screening in every contact.

Officer Mooney approached Larry Monroe at home. Monroe sued the City and officers under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging equal protection because race prompted the approach and because officers did not investigate similarly when suspects were described as white. He also alleged unlawful seizure through the encounter and taking bodily fluids for DNA. He sought class treatment of equal protection.

sections.title: Some individual theories survive while certification raises a participation problem
sections.cue: Trace the separate pleading and evidence decisions.
paragraphs: The district court dismissed the express racial-classification theory but retained the different-investigatory-methods theory. It dismissed encounter-as-seizure while allowing the bodily-fluids claim. An amendment added the uniform, lack of advice that Monroe could decline, home setting, and his beliefs about police-minority relations. The encounter theory was again dismissed. Equal-protection analysis included uncontested material outside the pleadings, with the appellate opinion addressing conversion to summary judgment where necessary; it was not wholly a allegations-only inquiry.

For certification, an officer’s affidavit reported Monroe saying counsel did not return calls, approached him about suing, and filed in his name without his learning until a newspaper report. It also reported that the action made him look bad and he wanted no damages against Mooney. The court set July 13, 2007 for memoranda and held a July 20 hearing. Monroe neither attended nor timely supplied an affidavit. His lawyer testified that she returned calls and he approached her, submitted his deposition, and said no further evidence would be offered.

Monroe filed a response affidavit July 23. The court rejected it as late and found him inadequate; his deposition showed little knowledge and inability to recognize his complaint. He then sought voluntary dismissal of remaining claims and agreed not to refile to obtain City consent and appellate jurisdiction, making dismissal effectively with prejudice.

sections.title: A representative need not master the law but must genuinely participate
paragraphs: The Fourth Circuit emphasized the plaintiff’s burden under Rule 23(a)(4) and the evidentiary nature of certification. Courts need not simply accept pleaded adequacy and may enforce deadlines. The prehearing deadline, completed hearing, and counsel’s statement justified excluding the late filing. Its response on calls was weak, and its desire-to-proceed assertion did not address a material district-court basis, so exclusion caused no material prejudice. This was no universal ban on late evidence.

Adequacy required enough interest, credibility, and understanding to avoid merely lending a name to counsel-controlled litigation, not mastery of every legal detail. The officer’s account, inability to recognize the complaint, and lack of filing knowledge raised substantial questions the limited rebuttal did not resolve. Privilege objections had also blocked questions about consideration and authorization of suit. The court relied on failure to meet the burden, not a rule that privilege objections automatically establish inadequacy.

sections.title: The pleaded home encounter does not plausibly establish a seizure
sections.cue: Keep this holding separate from taking bodily fluids.
paragraphs: Reviewing de novo under Twombly plausibility principles, the panel separated facts from labels such as coercion and nonconsent. Police approach and questions alone did not constitute seizure; the objective question was whether a reasonable person could disregard the officer and end the encounter.

Monroe’s subjective beliefs did not become controlling by invoking shared community experiences. The panel feared that approach would classify all police-minority encounters as seizures. No advice of a right to refuse, a uniform, and a home visit also occurred in consensual contacts. The actual allegations neither plausibly established seizure nor indicated discoverable facts beyond speculation. The ruling concerned that encounter theory, not every DNA collection or the merits of the separately dismissed bodily-fluid claim.

sections.title: Victims’ descriptions differ from the government inventing a racial profile
sections.cue: State both the principal and alternative equal-protection reasoning.
paragraphs: Monroe invoked Shelley v. Kraemer and Evans v. Newton, decisions about government involvement in private racial distinctions, and Grutter against treating race as merely one factor. The panel distinguished consistent descriptions of an actual assailant from officers creating a profile, choosing among conflicting racial accounts, or investigating Black residents as a group. Other characteristics and leads also guided the investigation. Enforcing exclusionary racial property covenants was different. Iqbal’s distinction between suspected links to crimes and incidental disparate impact also informed the court.

The panel acknowledged criticism of Brown v. City of Oneonta, another description-based investigation case, but found factual distinctions and no reason it changed this record’s result. It did not authorize every race-conscious police practice.

Alternatively, while recognizing incomplete record development might remain, it concluded strict scrutiny was satisfied on undisputed facts. Public protection from crime was compelling, and consistent victim descriptions, additional pertinent characteristics and information, and 190 contacts instead of a sweep of all Black male residents supported narrow tailoring.

On August 31, 2009, the court affirmed. Senior Judge C. Arlen Beam, sitting by designation, wrote for Judge Shedd and visiting District Judge Joseph F. Anderson, Jr., with no separate opinion. The voluntarily dismissed remaining theories were not adjudicated on their merits.
